strengths: The paper identifies a clear and important failure mode of current image generators: refracted content must remain consistent with directly visible scene content, rather than merely look glass-like. Addressing this constraint is useful and relatively underexplored.

Snellcaster is technically well motivated and reasonably original. It combines explicit Snell-law ray tracing, synchronized perspective/panoramic generation, Fresnel reflection blending, and per-step pixel-space warping in a coherent training-free pipeline.

The visual results are compelling. Across six indoor scenes, the method reproduces expected inversions and spatial distortions substantially better than Flux generation and inpainting. Supplementary examples with dog, cylinder, fox, sculpture, and pyramid meshes indicate applicability beyond spheres.

The quantitative evidence supports improved geometric fidelity: averaged masked PSNR rises from 11.24/11.18 for the two Flux baselines to 17.10, while LPIPS falls from 0.51 to 0.28. These improvements occur for every reported scene on both fidelity metrics.

Ablations cover detail-preserving averaging, Laplacian-pyramid warping, and time travel. Although the numerical differences are modest, the accompanying close-ups expose the distinct aliasing, boundary, and blending artifacts that these components address.

The manuscript is generally clear and provides prompts, principal equations, resolutions, sampling settings, hyperparameters, runtime, and placement heuristics, giving a useful basis for reproduction.
weaknesses: The empirical sample is very small: the principal quantitative evaluation contains only six prompts and apparently one generated result per prompt, with no repeated seeds, uncertainty estimates, or human evaluation. The complex-shape experiments are qualitative and largely reuse one scene, so robustness across scene geometry and generation variability remains weakly established.

The fidelity reference is not independent of the method: Blender and Snellcaster use the same estimated depth, object mesh, and source image, while Snellcaster explicitly injects pixels warped from that source. This makes the large PSNR/LPIPS advantage partly expected and does not establish correctness relative to real images or true scene geometry. Histogram-matched grayscale PSNR and a reference lacking correct lighting and reflections further limit the interpretation.

Some claims overstate the reported results. The supplement says performance is consistently stronger than both baselines across CLIP, PSNR, and LPIPS, but its own table shows lower CLIP than standard Flux for Kitchen and lower CLIP than both baselines for Living Room. Average ImageReward is also 0.59 versus 0.60 for standard Flux.

The automatic end-to-end claims receive limited validation. All six main prompts deliberately specify a large sphere on a central nearby tabletop, while object placement uses a tailored horizontal-surface heuristic. Several complex meshes come from RefRef rather than the claimed text-to-3D route, and no systematic evaluation is given for prompt decomposition, refractive-index inference, mesh generation, depth errors, or pose selection.

Physical accuracy is necessarily approximate: unseen geometry is replaced by a generated panorama treated as if centered across the object's surface, monocular depth supplies incomplete background geometry, and only a single uniform non-scattering object and dominant first reflection are modeled. The generative relighting post-process may also alter previously constrained pixels, but its effect on optical consistency is not isolated.

Reproducibility is incomplete because no code or released evaluation set is identified, and several important operational details—occlusion-mask construction, boundary handling, panorama initialization/coupling, and the exact scope of the relighting edit—are insufficiently specified for a faithful independent implementation.

strengths: The paper targets a concrete and underexplored failure mode of text-to-image models: transparent objects whose visible content is geometrically constrained by refraction. The combination of Snell-law ray tracing with synchronized perspective and panoramic generation is technically interesting and potentially useful.

The method is clearly described, with explicit warping, synchronization, Fresnel-blending, and denoising equations. Assumptions such as a single homogeneous, non-scattering refractive object are stated rather than hidden.

Qualitative comparisons show substantially more plausible geometric refraction than standard Flux generation or masked Flux inpainting, especially for spheres. The supplementary results also demonstrate applicability to several non-spherical meshes and different refractive indices.
The paper includes useful implementation details, prompts, runtime, qualitative component ablations, and quantitative comparisons using both perceptual and reference-based metrics.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is much too narrow to support the broad robustness and physical-accuracy claims. The central evaluation contains only six hand-designed prompts, apparently one generated example per prompt, with no repeated seeds, uncertainty estimates, human perceptual study, real-image comparison, or evaluation on an established benchmark.

The principal PSNR/LPIPS evaluation is partly circular. The Blender reference and the proposed method use the same estimated RGBD geometry, object mesh, material parameters, and ray-tracing correspondences; evaluation also excludes rays hitting unobserved surfaces and applies grayscale conversion and histogram matching. The resulting improvement mainly verifies that explicitly applying the same geometric warp matches that warp better than unconstrained Flux, rather than demonstrating realistic image generation under independent ground truth.

The baseline set is inadequate for isolating the contribution. Both baselines are generic Flux variants that are not supplied with the geometry and optical parameters given to Snellcaster. There is no direct-rendering/compositing baseline, rendering followed by harmonization or diffusion refinement, synchronization without the panorama, or other geometry-conditioned construction. Consequently, the experiments do not show that the proposed synchronized diffusion procedure is preferable to simpler use of the privileged inputs.

The claimed optical accuracy is overstated. Hidden scene geometry is represented by a generated panorama centered at one point, which ignores spatial parallax across the object's surface, while visible geometry comes from a single-view depth mesh. Fresnel blending models only a dominant reflection and does not account for transmission losses and reflected contributions at every interface along a multi-interface path. Absorption, scattering, heterogeneous materials, and multiple transparent objects are also excluded.

The panorama's alleged consistency and benefit are not directly evaluated. No ablation removes cross-view synchronization or replaces panorama content with an independent completion, and no geometric or semantic consistency metric is reported for unseen regions. These are central claimed contributions, unlike the presented ablations of largely inherited sampling/warping components.

The component ablation evidence is weak. It uses one visual scene, while quantitative differences for DPA and LPW are negligible; removing LPW even slightly improves PSNR and LPIPS. Thus the statement that every component contributes meaningfully is not supported by the reported measurements.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful prompts and hyperparameters. Important choices—including depth-to-mesh construction, occlusion-mask computation, boundary handling, exact panorama synchronization, object scale and pose heuristics, and the post-processing model or fine-tuning procedure—are insufficiently specified, and no code or release commitment is provided.

Overall, the idea has merit and the qualitative results are promising, but the evaluation design does not independently substantiate the paper's main claims of robust, physically accurate generation. These are consequential scientific limitations rather than presentation refinements, so the current balance favors rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and underexplored failure mode of text-to-image models: transparent objects must remain consistent with scene content visible both directly and through refraction. Enforcing Snell-law correspondences during generation is well motivated and produces visibly more plausible refractions than standard Flux and Flux inpainting.

The method is technically coherent and training-free. It combines explicit ray tracing, Fresnel-based reflection/refraction mixing, and synchronized perspective and panoramic generation to handle both observed background surfaces and content outside the original view. The panorama branch is a useful solution to otherwise unconstrained rays.

The qualitative results show convincing improvements across six indoor scenes and several additional object geometries. In particular, the expected inversions and spatial distortions are substantially closer to the Blender references, while the baselines frequently hallucinate unrelated content, omit the object, or produce hollow-looking geometry.

The quantitative evidence is directionally consistent with the visual results: average masked PSNR improves from about 11.2 to 17.1 dB and masked LPIPS from 0.51 to 0.28 relative to both Flux baselines. The paper also reports full per-scene results, component ablations, refractive-index variations, runtime, prompts, and major hyperparameters.

The manuscript is clear and unusually candid about important assumptions and metric limitations, including imperfect lighting in the Blender references, missing unobserved surfaces, and the inability of generic preference metrics to measure optical correctness.
weaknesses: The primary quantitative evaluation is very small: it contains only six prompts and apparently one generated example per scene, without repeated seeds, uncertainty estimates, or human evaluation. Thus, the reported gains are compelling demonstrations but weak evidence of robustness across prompt distributions and generation stochasticity.

The Blender pseudo-ground truth is constructed from the same estimated RGBD geometry and object model used by the method. This appropriately tests adherence to its own ray-traced correspondences, but does not establish correctness relative to real transparent-object photographs or independently measured geometry. Grayscale evaluation with histogram matching further removes color and lighting errors, and the reference omits valid reflected and unseen content.

Generality remains only partially supported. Most quantitative experiments use one glass sphere; the five additional shapes and refractive-index sweep are qualitative and concentrated in similar indoor settings. The method assumes a single non-scattering object with uniform refractive index, an available watertight mesh, reliable monocular depth, and heuristic pose placement. Failures from inaccurate geometry, pose, material estimates, nearby surfaces, or the center-panorama approximation are not systematically evaluated.

Several components are adapted from prior synchronization and warping methods, so the originality lies mainly in their physically grounded assembly for refraction rather than a fundamentally new generative formulation. Nevertheless, this application and the treatment of unseen refracted/reflected rays constitute a meaningful contribution.

Reproducibility is reasonable at the manuscript level but not complete: prompts, hyperparameters, and runtime are supplied, yet no code or exact seed list is provided, and the pipeline depends on multiple large external systems, including Flux, MoGe-2, TRELLIS, an LLM, and a relighting model. The post-processing model can also change object appearance after physical synchronization, but its effect is not isolated quantitatively.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and underexplored failure mode of image generators: transparent objects must reproduce scene content through geometrically constrained refraction rather than merely look glass-like. This is an important computer-vision/graphics problem with plausible downstream value for image editing and compositing.

Snellcaster is technically well motivated and reasonably original. It combines Snell-law ray tracing, Fresnel reflection/refraction blending, synchronized perspective–panorama generation, detail-preserving blending, and Laplacian-pyramid warping in a coherent training-free pipeline.

The qualitative evidence is compelling. Figures 3, 9, and 10 show substantially more plausible background inversions and distortions than FLUX-based and other text-to-image baselines, including for several non-spherical geometries. The method also produces reasonable content for rays reaching unseen regions.

The reported evaluation is broader than a handful of examples: Table 1 covers 300 scene–object combinations and shows large gains in the geometry-oriented metrics, from roughly 12–13 dB to 16.51 dB PSNR and from 0.47–0.53 to 0.24 LPIPS, while retaining broadly comparable semantic scores.

The reflection and panorama ablations, additional component ablations, refractive-index sweep, and two captured-scene examples collectively probe several aspects of the pipeline. The authors also state important assumptions and limitations, including one homogeneous non-scattering object, approximate geometry, and incomplete lighting treatment.
The manuscript is generally clear and visually effective. The physical construction, synchronization mechanism, and role of the auxiliary panorama are understandable from the equations and flowchart.
weaknesses: The main quantitative comparison is partly structurally favorable to the proposed method. The Blender reference and Snellcaster both use the same object-free RGBD estimate, object mesh, and ray-tracing geometry, whereas most baselines generate an independent full scene from text. Matching random seeds across different generators does not align scene content. Consequently, PSNR/LPIPS against the Blender rendering are not meaningful measures for the full text-to-image baselines; the inpainting baseline is better paired, but it still receives substantially less geometric information. Geometry-conditioned rendering or editing baselines would make the central comparison more diagnostic.

The claimed optical accuracy is stronger than what the pipeline establishes. Monocular estimated depth, a panorama represented from one point near the object center, first-order reflection only, and generative relighting are approximations rather than a physically complete image formation model. Shadows and caustics are hallucinated by a post-processing editor, and the paper explicitly omits absorption, scattering, heterogeneous materials, and multiple transparent objects. The contribution is better characterized as geometry-guided, optically more plausible generation than fully accurate light transport.

The pseudo-ground-truth evaluation has important limitations acknowledged by the authors: it uses mismatched lighting, lacks reflected background content, masks unobserved surfaces, converts to grayscale with histogram matching, and is generated from estimated rather than true scene geometry. These choices weaken the evidential force of the otherwise large metric gains, particularly for the final relighted output.

There is no human perceptual study or physics-focused judgment study. CLIP and ImageReward do not assess refraction correctness, while the synthetic pixel metrics are coupled to the method's own geometric construction. The real-world evaluation contains only two qualitative pairs and provides no calibrated geometric or perceptual measurement.

Several ablation effects are quantitatively small or mixed. In Table 2, removing reflection or panorama synchronization changes PSNR by only 0.10–0.23 dB and improves ImageReward; in Table 4, removing Laplacian-pyramid warping slightly improves PSNR and LPIPS, while removing time travel improves CLIP and ImageReward. The qualitative ablation is largely a single scene, so it does not firmly establish every component's general contribution.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives major hyperparameters and prompts, but does not provide code or sufficiently precise specifications for camera calibration, depth-to-mesh construction, mesh scale/orientation, occlusion masks, panorama boundaries, automated failure handling, and all preprocessing costs. The 126-second runtime excludes preprocessing, and the relighting stage samples 20 edits and selects one, making the full computational cost and exact protocol unclear.

The automatic text-to-object story is not fully validated end to end. Complex-object examples use clean RefRef meshes, while only limited evidence is given that TRELLIS outputs are consistently watertight and optically usable. Errors from LLM-derived refractive indices, generated geometry, monocular depth, segmentation, scale, and pose are not separately evaluated.

strengths: The paper addresses a concrete and underexplored failure mode of text-to-image models: transparent objects whose appearance is constrained by refraction and reflection. The problem is relevant to computer vision and graphics.

Snellcaster is a technically coherent combination of ray tracing, Snell/Fresnel optics, estimated scene geometry, and synchronized perspective/panorama generation. Applying the constraints during denoising is more interesting than simple post-processing.

The manuscript is generally clear and includes prompts, principal hyperparameters, per-scene results, runtime, several object geometries, refractive-index examples, and component ablations.
weaknesses: The central quantitative comparison is materially confounded. The Blender pseudo-reference is constructed from the same object-free image, estimated geometry, object mesh, refractive index, and ray-tracing assumptions that directly guide Snellcaster. In contrast, most baselines independently generate a different scene from text. Masked PSNR/LPIPS against Snellcaster's source scene therefore strongly favor the proposed method and do not isolate physical accuracy. Using the same random seed does not establish pixel or layout correspondence across different generators.

The comparison lacks strong, task-matched baselines. A simple Blender-rendered or composited insertion using the recovered geometry, a post-hoc physics warp, and geometry-conditioned editing methods would clarify whether synchronized generation provides benefits beyond directly injecting the constructed reference. Only FLUX inpainting receives the object-free image, while the other baselines solve a substantially less constrained problem.

The claim that the method improves physical fidelity “without sacrificing text alignment and image aesthetics” is contradicted by Table 1. Snellcaster's CLIP score (32.85) trails several baselines, including SD3.5 at 34.56, while its ImageReward score (-0.32) is substantially below FLUX.2 (0.18), Qwen (0.01), and SD3.5 (0.08). No human preference or realism study supports the aesthetics claim.

Evidence on real imagery is inadequate for the paper's broad realism and optical-accuracy claims. Only two qualitative real-scene pairs are shown, with no calibrated geometry, quantitative correspondence measure, or human assessment. These examples cannot establish that the generated spheres match the actual photographed refractions.

The ablations provide weak evidence for several design choices. Removing reflections or panorama synchronization changes PSNR by only 0.10 and 0.23 dB, respectively; removing Laplacian pyramid warping actually slightly improves PSNR and LPIPS; and multiple ablations improve ImageReward. The qualitative crops suggest artifact reduction, but the assertion that every component contributes meaningfully is stronger than the reported quantitative evidence.

The method's description of being optically accurate is overstated. It depends on monocular estimated geometry, treats a panorama at the object's center as the environment seen from all surface points, keeps only the dominant first reflection, and excludes absorption, scattering, heterogeneous media, and multiple transparent objects. These approximations can introduce systematic parallax and transport errors, particularly for large or nearby non-spherical objects.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful implementation details. The paper does not fully specify camera recovery, object scale and orientation, construction and closure of the depth mesh and bounding box, occlusion masks, or all blending details. The stochastic LLM/TRELLIS/SAM preprocessing and the 20-candidate relighting-selection process further require code, model versions, and exact selection definitions that are not supplied.

Overall, the idea and qualitative behavior are worthwhile, but the evaluation does not convincingly demonstrate the claimed optical realism because the main metric is closely coupled to the method's inputs and is applied unfairly to independently generated baselines. This evidence gap is consequential enough that the current balance favors rejection.

strengths: The paper tackles a clear and important failure mode of modern image generators: transparent objects often contain refracted content inconsistent with the visible scene. The problem is well motivated and relevant to physically grounded image generation.

Snellcaster is technically coherent and combines explicit ray tracing, Snell's law, Fresnel reflection, perspective-panorama synchronization, and iterative flow-model guidance in a novel and useful pipeline. In particular, using a generated panorama to supply plausible content for occluded and out-of-frame rays is a strong idea.

The qualitative results are compelling. Across spheres and more complex geometries, the method usually preserves recognizable scene structure under refraction substantially better than generic generation and inpainting baselines.

The evaluation includes 300 scene-object combinations, multiple contemporary generators, component ablations, refractive-index variations, complex objects, and two real-image demonstrations. Table 1 shows large improvements in masked PSNR and LPIPS, while the reported CLIP degradation is relatively modest.

The method is training-free with respect to the proposed synchronization procedure, and the manuscript explains the principal geometry, warps, blending equations, hyperparameters, prompts, and runtime. The presentation and figures are generally clear.
weaknesses: The main physical-fidelity evaluation is structurally favorable to the proposed method. The Blender reference is rendered from the same object-free RGBD image, mesh, pose, and ray-tracing geometry that Snellcaster explicitly warps, whereas unconstrained text-to-image baselines do not preserve that image's pixel geometry. Consequently, their masked PSNR/LPIPS comparison—especially for non-inpainting baselines—does not cleanly isolate realistic refraction quality. Evaluation on independently rendered synthetic scenes, controlled composites, or a larger paired real dataset would provide stronger evidence.

Some conclusions overstate the reported metrics. Snellcaster's CLIP score (32.85) is below several baselines, and its ImageReward (-0.32) is below all except FLUX Inpaint, so the claim that it 'better aligns with the text prompts' is not supported by Table 1. The results instead show a reasonable fidelity-versus-generic-quality tradeoff.

Evidence for several individual components is limited. Removing reflections or panorama synchronization changes PSNR only from 18.21 to 18.11 or 17.98 and LPIPS from 0.24 to 0.25; the DPA and LPW ablations are similarly small, with LPW removal even slightly improving PSNR and LPIPS. ImageReward often improves under ablation. The qualitative ablations use only a small number of examples, so strong component-level claims should be interpreted cautiously.

The scope is constrained to one non-scattering object with a uniform refractive index, known/generated watertight geometry, and heuristic placement on a horizontal support. It omits absorption, heterogeneous or nested materials, and native illumination or shadow transport. A panorama centered at one point also approximates rays originating across the object's surface and can become inaccurate for nearby geometry and strong parallax.

Real-world validation consists of only two qualitative pairs, with no user study or correspondence-based measurement. This is insufficient to establish robustness to real depth errors, camera calibration, imperfect object pose, and complex lighting.

Reproducibility depends on a long chain of large external systems, including MoGe-2, TRELLIS, SAM 3, ChatGPT, FLUX, and a harmonization model. The relighting stage generates 20 candidates and selects one using PSNR, adding substantial cost and a selection procedure that is not fully characterized; the reported 126-second runtime also excludes preprocessing.
